titre: Tulip Mania in 1637, a Crisis Without Ruin
accroche: In February 1637, the price of tulip bulbs collapses in the Netherlands. Legend speaks of shattered fortunes; the archives say otherwise.
contenu_vulgarise:
On February 3, 1637, in Haarlem, an auctioneer puts a lot of tulip bulbs up for sale and finds no one to buy them. Within days, the market that had run away with itself all winter collapses: contracts on the most common bulbs lose most of their value. At the height of the fever, a single Semper Augustus bulb (a striped variety, produced by a virus that damages the tulip, though no one yet knows it) trades for the equivalent of 10,000 florins, about thirty years of a skilled craftsman's wages. The image that has survived, peddled for two centuries: an entire nation, from merchant to chimney sweep, ruined in a single winter by flower madness.

## A Legend Older Than the Economics That Studies It

This image does not come from a 17th-century economist but from Dutch Calvinist pamphlets published at the very time of the crisis, which denounce less a financial disaster than a sin: pride and greed punished by the fall. Two centuries later, the Scottish writer Charles Mackay takes up and amplifies this account in *Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds* (1841), without checking its sources, and makes it the first canonical example of a speculative bubble. It is this version, Mackay's, that has since made its way into most textbooks.

At the turn of the 2000s, the historian Anne Goldgar combs through the notarial minutes, sales registers, and trial files of the Netherlands of the period. In 2007 she draws the opposite conclusion: the trade in rare tulips never mobilized more than a small circle of merchants and well-off craftsmen, never Dutch society as a whole; and among all the buyers and sellers identified, she finds no more than half a dozen cases of financial difficulty, without even the tulips being clearly the cause. “I haven't found anyone who went bankrupt,” she sums up. The economist Peter Garber reaches a similar conclusion by another route: a comparable price drop struck hyacinth bulbs when they were introduced in the 19th century, an ordinary phenomenon of a rare novelty losing its rarity, and most of the trading in the winter of 1636-1637 was done on forward contracts, with no money paid up front, so that the price collapse cost only a minority any real money.

## What Really Happened

In late February 1637, the merchants gathered in Amsterdam reach a compromise: contracts signed before December 1636 remain due, while later ones can be canceled for 10% of their value. The trade of the Dutch East India Company, herring fishing, weaving: none of these pillars of the Dutch economy shows the slightest tremor that year. Something did happen in 1637: a crisis of confidence within a merchant guild, settled by negotiation. It is not the national ruin that the word “tulip mania” continues to denote.

citation.texte: I haven't found anyone who went bankrupt.

carte.punch: Tulip mania ruined almost no one. The archives have been saying so since 2007.
carte.idee: The legend of a Holland ruined by tulip madness comes from moralizing pamphlets and a 19th-century book. The notarial archives combed by the historian Anne Goldgar show only a handful of well-off merchants in difficulty, and no tremor in the rest of the economy.

quiz.question: What does the historian Anne Goldgar's study of the Dutch notarial archives reveal?
choix: That the tulip trade led to the bankruptcy of several major Amsterdam banks
That the trade involved only a small circle of merchants, with no widespread ruin
That tulip prices never actually fell in 1637
That the crisis immediately collapsed the trade of the Dutch East India Company
quiz.explication: Goldgar found only a handful of cases of financial difficulty tied to tulips, within a small circle of merchants and well-off craftsmen, and no major pillar of the Dutch economy, from herring fishing to colonial trade, shows a tremor that year.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the image of a Holland ruined by tulip mania come from?
choix: From notarial minutes combed by Anne Goldgar in 2007
From Calvinist pamphlets of the period, amplified by Charles Mackay in 1841
From an official report by the Amsterdam merchants in 1637
From the economist Peter Garber's work on hyacinth bulbs
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The account comes from moralizing Calvinist pamphlets published during the crisis, taken up and amplified two centuries later by Charles Mackay in an 1841 book, without checking the sources.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the compromise reached in Amsterdam in late February 1637?
choix: The total cancellation of all tulip contracts
Full reimbursement of all losses by the Crown
Contracts before December 1636 due, later ones cancelable for 10%
A permanent ban on the tulip bulb trade
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The merchants gathered in Amsterdam decide that contracts signed before December 1636 remain due in full, while later ones can be canceled for 10% of their value.
